1:
The title carries its own authority: Henry notes that it is from heaven and not of men, and that the prophet's name means the servant of the Lord, since God reveals his secrets to his servants the prophets. Other prophets are traced no further than a father; this pedigree runs back four generations, and Ellicott takes the Hizkiah at the head of it for Hezekiah, possibly the king of that name. Keil and Delitzsch argue the point: because only the father is named as a rule, a man carried back that far must have been celebrated, and the absence of the title king of Judah is explained by its following at once with Josiah. The objection that only two generations stand between the two kings falls away when Manasseh reigned fifty-five years, nearly two generations by himself. Wesley agrees that the prophet was great-grandson to Hezekiah and was contemporary with Jeremiah and Ezekiel. Henry adds the practical gain: descended from that pious prince and so of the royal family, he could the better reprove the folly of the king's children. Calvin doubts one inference. The rule that a prophet who names his father was himself son of a prophet is not well founded, since four ancestors can hardly all have been prophets and Scripture says nothing of them; the name of Amon is set down not for honour but for reproach.

Clarke fixes the date from the disorders described. The prophet must have spoken before the reformation Josiah made in the eighteenth year of his reign, and since he predicts the destruction of Nineveh the prophecy belongs near the beginning of that reign. Henry leaves both possibilities open, and finds either instructive: if Zephaniah spoke early, his preaching may have helped the reformation forward, for reformation prospers when magistrates and ministers each do their part; if late, we see how a corrupt people relapse once the first heat of reform wears off.

Then the sentence, without preamble. Gill hears a general denunciation whose particulars follow, and offers the Hebrew idiom, in gathering I will gather, all good things out of the land, every necessary of life, so that the land is left naked and bare; the instrument is the Chaldeans. Clarke says by war and by pestilence, the waters infected and the fowls dying. Keil and Delitzsch see judgment threatened over the whole earth and falling especially upon Judah and Jerusalem. Henry compares the deluge, when every living substance was destroyed, and draws the moral: those who fly high as the fowls of heaven, or hide close as the fishes of the sea, are not out of the enemy's reach. Ellicott takes the stumblingblocks as the enticements to sin together with the sinners, refusing the sense of a ruin the word bears elsewhere. Calvin meets the obvious protest, that innocent animals ought to have been spared. They were created for man's use and must undergo a lot common with him; the whole world was made subject to corruption not willingly but through the contagion of Adam's fall. The purpose is also rhetorical, to rouse a torpid people: if wrath lays hold on creatures that have committed no sins, shall the guilty escape unpunished?
4:
Gill weighs the preposition. It is not to Judah, as beckoning them to come and hearken, for that call had been made and rejected; nor over Judah, to protect and defend; it is upon Judah, exerting power and executing vengeance, and when that hand is stretched out it cannot be turned back. Under Judah he includes Benjamin, the ten tribes having gone into captivity in Hezekiah's time many years before. Calvin explains the stretched hand as the language of unusual action: God performs all things by his command alone, but he is said to stretch forth his hand when the work is remarkable, as a man moves only his hand for a slight task and prepares his arms for a difficult one. He notes whom the threat now reaches. Jerusalem thought itself exempt, because there the sacrifices were performed, there the royal city stood, and God had testified that his habitation should be there for ever; so the prophet turns and says in effect that there is no need to ask who the wicked are, for the race of Abraham that flatters itself on its excellency is the very people meant.

The remnant of Baal is read two ways. Clarke and Wesley take it of whatever survived Josiah's purge, and Clarke refers the promise partly to that reformation itself. Ellicott resists the inference that a large part of the worship had already been overthrown; the word means only that the thing shall be so utterly abolished that not even a remnant is left. Calvin accounts for a remnant surviving a thorough king: the images were no longer seen in the temple or the streets or the high places, but the people cherished their old corruptions at home, restrained only by fear of men, and their sin was the heavier for refusing to follow a pious leader. On the Chemarims the voices agree in substance and differ in derivation. Wesley offers the black garments they went in, or the swarthy colour got from the black smoke of incense, and makes them door-keepers and sextons of Baal; Clarke calls them the black-robed priests of different idols. Ellicott identifies them from the record of the purge as the idolatrous priests ordained to burn incense in the high places, and adds that the very name of these intruders is to go. On the priests named with them Ellicott parts from Wesley, who reads simply the priests of Baal; Ellicott thinks a section of the lawful priesthood is meant, men who had winked at the false establishment.

Gill and Calvin agree on the housetops: the flat roofs gave a full view, and the worshippers supposed that the nearer they came the more they were seen. Clarke calls this the most ancient and common species of idolatry, and the one with the greatest semblance of reason. Ellicott renders the next clause as worshippers who swear to Jehovah and who swear also by Malcham, allegiance divided between the true God and the false, and takes the name for a combination of their king with Moloch, elsewhere an Ammonite deity, perhaps identical with the planet Saturn. Calvin says the mixture is the offence: they did not openly reject the God who redeemed them, but blended his worship with their own inventions, and God will not suffer his worship to be thus profaned. Of those turned back, Gill thinks of men who renewed the covenant under Josiah and then revolted; Clarke glosses the last clause as having no desire to know his will; Calvin refuses them the shield of ignorance, since the law had shown the way plainly and they turned willfully aside. Ellicott records an observation that the list descends by steps from gross external to refined internal apostasy, ending with those merely indifferent to religion.
7:
Clarke hears an interjection rather than a sentence: the Hebrew particle answers to our hush, and remonstrance is now useless, since there was time to acquaint yourselves with God and the crying comes too late. Ellicott renders it literally, Hush at the presence of the Lord God, and notes the same peculiar phrase standing elsewhere in the prophets. Gill fills out what the silence forbids: do not dispute the point with him, do not offer reasons against his proceedings or set out to disprove their justice, but stand in awe of the omniscient and omnipotent God and let not one murmuring word come out of the mouth. Wesley addresses it to the same man, thou that murmurest against God. Calvin makes the silence a settled disposition. It means submission, and its opposite is contumacy, which is always clamorous; while men seek to be wise of themselves and will not acquiesce in the word, all places are full of noise and life runs to and fro without restraint. Here, though, the demand is fitted to the occasion. The prophet saw God's judgment despised as nothing, and means to say that the sentence has been spoken and the execution is at hand.

Henry draws the terms of the visit. Those who will not improve the presence of God with them as a Father, but sin that presence away, may expect his presence as a Judge, to call them to account for contempt of his grace; men have their day now, when they take liberty to do as they please, but God's day is at hand. That day is called his sacrifice, and Henry reads the figure closely: to punish presumptuous sinners is itself a sacrifice to the justice of God, some reparation to his injured honour, and those who brought their offerings to other gods are justly made victims to the true God. On a sacrifice day the slaughter was great, and men shall be killed as fast as lambs for the altar and with as little regret. Clarke lays out the two parts of such a festival, the victims offered and their blood poured out before the altar, and then the invited people feasting on what was offered.

Who the invited are is disputed. Ellicott, who observes that the word for sacrifice already carries the idea of the feast in which the remains were consumed, renders the clause more literally as he has consecrated his invited ones, and identifies them with the foreign nations chosen as ministers of chastisement, bidden as it were to banquet upon an apostate people. Henry names them outright as the Chaldeans, guests prepared and invited to glut their revenge with slaughter and their covetousness with plunder. Wesley takes the guests otherwise: not armies but the beasts of the field and the fowls of the air, summoned to eat the flesh and drink the blood. Calvin closes on the purpose of the warning rather than its imagery. The prophet reminds them that God is prepared to execute vengeance so that, if there be any hope of repentance, they may seek in time to return into favour with him, and if not, that they may be left without excuse.
8:
Gill sets the clock: the day of the sacrifice is the time within which the slaughter begins and ends. Keil and Delitzsch read the following verses as a deliberate survey, three double verses naming three classes that differ in civil position and in attitude toward God, so that no rank shall be able to plead exemption; the princes and superior servants of the king, who copy foreign customs and oppress the people, are threatened first. Who the king's children are is disputed. Wesley takes them for the sons and grandsons of Josiah and follows their several ends, Jehoahaz dying a captive in Egypt, Jehoiakim in Babylon and buried with the burial of an ass, Jeconiah a captive, and Zedekiah faring worse still; Clarke adds that no reign after Josiah saw prosperity, and that Zedekiah and the king's children were massacred at Riblah when Nebuchadnezzar had taken Jerusalem. Ellicott hesitates, because on his dating those princes would have been mere children who could hardly yet have provoked such a word, and prefers to understand the king's brothers or uncles. Wesley notes the irony that the great ones, who dreamed of shifting better than others, fell with the first.

On the strange apparel Ellicott thinks of the luxurious dress of foreign nations, perhaps the gorgeous apparel of Assyria and Babylonia, and explains why clothing should be a mark of apostasy at all: the national dress with its riband at the fringe had been appointed so that the people might look upon it and remember the commandments of the Lord and do them. Clarke doubts the charge is about dress. He takes it rather of embracing idolatrous customs and heathen usages, new habits acquired and worn at all times and in everything as they wore their clothes. Wesley says simply the garb of foreigners, imitated by wanton Jews.

The leaping on the threshold is the obscurest clause in the chapter, and three readings are offered. Gill mentions and sets aside a ludicrous sense, of servants who made sport by dancing and leaping and brought their masters gain; he allows either a rash and irreverent entry into the house of God, or an idolatrous rite. Clarke and Ellicott settle on the rite, tracing it to the temples of Dagon, whose worshippers after their idol fell and was broken on the threshold would no more set a foot on it but stepped or leaped over. Clarke thinks the Philistines themselves are meant, and reports a quite different explanation drawn from the customs of the Arabs, who rode into houses and carried off what they could, which is why doors in several parts of the East are made low; he cites an account of the Persians so oppressing the Armenians. Ellicott records that second reading too, in which leaping the threshold is a sudden rushing into houses to steal, and the offenders are servants of the king extorting treasure from dependants by violence and fraud, but doubts that such practices would have been tolerated among the retainers of a pious king, unless he had not yet gained authority to check them. Their masters' houses divides the voices again: Ellicott would render their lord's house, the temple of the idol-deity, filled with violence and deceit by offerings got through fraud and oppression, while Wesley thinks of the oppressing kings whose officers these were, or of public officers and judges whose servants spoiled the poor by force, false accusation, and suborned evidence.
10:
Gill anchors the threat before the topography: this shall surely come to pass because the Lord has said it, and not one word of his shall pass away. Calvin explains why a prophet turns cartographer at all. A lively representation touches the feelings as a plain narration does not, so the ruin of Jerusalem is not merely announced but set before the eyes as a scene. The three places named, with a fourth added after, he takes to be quarters lying opposite one another, so that no corner of the city should be quiet when the Lord roused up war and the people would find every direction full of crying and howling; he rejects the suggestion that the hills mean palaces as inconsistent with the passage. Ellicott names the hills as Mount Zion and Mount Moriah, the sites of the old city and the Temple, so that every part of Jerusalem is included; Wesley says only, the hills on which the city stood.

The fish gate is placed by Clarke opposite Joppa, which he thinks explains why news of the irruption of the Chaldean army should arrive there first; Calvin will guess no further than that a fish-pond or a fish-market stood near it. Wesley claims more, that the Babylonians actually entered the city by that gate. On the second the voices divide. Clarke and Ellicott supply the noun and read the second or lower city, the newer quarter; Wesley makes it a gate in the second of three walls that fortified the city on that side. Calvin records the majority opinion of interpreters, that the word denotes the place where the priests expounded the law and gave themselves to its study. Wesley alone attends to the crashing, hearing in it things broken into shivers, perhaps the noise of doors and windows and closets and chests broken open.

Maktesh divides them further. Gill reports it as the name of a street, lying low in the hollow of the city and shaped like a mortar, from which the word may come, unless it was named from people who used mortars for pounding spice. Calvin insists it is not a proper name at all but a description, the hollow, and argues from the verb that the hollow shape is the root sense and the pounding derived from it rather than the reverse; he thinks merchants would naturally have their streets on level ground, since they have goods to carry. Wesley calls it simply the lower town. Ellicott locates it in the valley that ran through the city, a quarter described by an old historian as full of houses, and reports two further guesses, that the name alludes to the din of the trade carried on there, and that the prophet coined it to signify how everything in Jerusalem should be bruised to pieces as in a mortar. Clarke reports the same figure, the inhabitants pounded to death as grain is pounded, along with a tradition that this was the quarter where they hulled rice and corn. On the merchant people Ellicott notes that the phrase is literally the people of Canaan, a term used elsewhere for traders and so not to be held to its original sense; Calvin records another reading, that the Jews are called Canaan because they had grown degenerate and more like the Canaanites than the fathers from whom they descended. Clarke lists the class plainly as merchants, moneychangers, usurers and rich men, and Wesley says those laden with silver brought it with them to pay for what they bought.
12:
Calvin turns the searching with candles into a picture of plunder. A man who means to strip a city enters the houses and takes what he finds, but if he suspects hidden treasure he goes down into the secret cells, and where there is no light he lights a candle and looks carefully here and there so as to overlook nothing; God intimates by the comparison that Jerusalem would be so plundered that nothing whatever would remain. Both he and Wesley guard the figure at once: God speaks after the manner of men, since nothing is hidden from him, and he borrows such comparisons because he could not otherwise express what we need to know. Calvin adds the reason for the borrowing, that the world deals with God as men deal with one another and supposes he can be deceived by craft, which folly he here laughs to scorn. Gill agrees that the searching must be understood consistently with the omniscience of God, and points to how it was executed: what the Lord says he will do he did by instruments, by the Chaldeans, to whom the gates of the city and the doors of houses and their innermost recesses were opened and plundered, so that sins men thought secret were exposed. Clarke states the sense in a line, a universal and thorough search.

The lees are read as a figure of stagnation. Wesley alludes to liquors which, not being poured from vessel to vessel to refine them, grow thick and foul; Ellicott takes it of wine gone harsh from standing too long, and calls the men selfish sybarites whose souls have stagnated in undisturbed prosperity, and whose inexperience of affliction has led them to deny the agency of God in the world, like the rich fool in the parable. Clarke describes them as careless and satisfied with the goods of this life, trusting in riches and wholly irreligious, and gives their creed a philosophical pedigree: while acknowledging that there is a God, they think, like the Aristotelians, that he is so supremely happy in contemplating his own excellences that he counts it beneath his dignity to concern himself with the affairs of mortals. Calvin allows that the words might be taken only of the rich who flattered themselves in prosperity, but judges from what follows that something more atrocious is in view, and prefers to join the two charges: men inebriated with prosperity grow hardened, as others contract hardness by labour, and collect such lees through too much quietness and abundance that they become wholly stupid and can be touched by no truth made known to them.

The sentence follows from the security. Gill notes that the riches they trusted in, and on whose account they denied divine Providence, become the enemy's booty, and that the Lord has many ways of stripping men of what they enjoy and giving it to others. Clarke names the Chaldeans as the takers, and states the loss twice over: the houses they built they shall not inhabit, and of the wine of the vineyards they planted they shall not drink. Both Ellicott and Calvin recognise the words as the law's own curse on apostasy returning upon them. Calvin makes the principle explicit, that the prophets were interpreters of the law and differ from Moses only in applying his general truth to their own time; God had not threatened this evil in vain, and the people would find by experience that the fruit of the land and their habitations and the other comforts of life really would be transferred to others.
14:
What day is meant is settled first. Gill denies it is the day of judgment; it is the day of God's vengeance on the Jews by the Chaldeans, though it bore some resemblance to that day and may be so called, as the later destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans had its likeness too. Henry says the same in stronger terms, calling it a specimen of the day of judgment, a kind of doom's-day. Clarke gives it dates, from the death of the good king Josiah, slain at Megiddo, to the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar. Calvin finds three things packed into the opening clause: that the evils were not only from men but especially from God, so that the Jews should consider his hand when he strikes; that the day would be terrible, in order to touch stupid hearts; and that it was at hand, since men extend time to cherish their sins, and while unable to shake off all sense of religion imagine a long distance between themselves and God, finding ease in the imagination. They ought not, he says, to judge from the present state of things what God will do.

The nearness is pressed by repetition. Gill hears the word doubled for confirmation and to rouse the thoughtless who put the evil day far from them, and notes that the day is said to make great haste and fly faster than time usually does, though time in common has wings ascribed to it. Henry supplies the tone: the prophet gives the alarm like one in earnest, as a man wakes a household with the cry of Fire when the danger is at the next door, and it is madness for those to slumber whose damnation slumbers not.

Then the noise of it. Ellicott would render the clause Hark to the day, and identifies what is heard as the cry of the baffled warrior, unable either to fight or to flee. Henry hears the same and marks the reversal, that the very report of the day should make mighty men cry for fear as children do. Clarke praises the passage as a beautiful amplification of the disasters coming on Jerusalem, in which invasion and attack and carnage and confusion, the din of the trumpet, the cries of the people and the groans of the dying are set out with great force. Gill divides the wrath in two, the wrath of God against his people, whose judgments are its effects, and the wrath and cruelty of the Chaldeans exercised in a furious manner. Ellicott notes that clouds and thick darkness are the terms used when Jehovah revealed himself on Sinai. Henry reads the darkness as the extinction of hope: everything shall look dismal, and there shall not be the least gleam of comfort or glimpse of hope; look round, and it is all black, and the thick clouds are big with storms and tempests. Wesley reduces the whole verse to a phrase, a day of unparalleled calamities. Calvin explains why so many terms are heaped together. Hypocrites extenuate God's vengeance, and though they promise themselves nothing of his favour they imagine he may be pacified without trouble, and so deride the vengeance they do not expect to escape; the piled figures are meant to constrain some fear in men who wilfully delude themselves. The flesh, he says, is secure only while it has coverts in which to withdraw from the presence of God, and wishes for no rest but the forgetfulness of him, whereas true confidence keeps within measure because it is founded on his word.
16:
Gill hears the trumpet as the enemy's, sounding the alarm of war against the fenced cities of Judea, which were taken before Jerusalem, calling and gathering the soldiers, animating them to the assault, and blowing at last in a way of triumph as expressive of victory. Ellicott adjusts the second noun, which is better rendered a war cry. On the distress Gill narrows the reference: not men in general but the men of Judea and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and especially those in the fenced cities and high towers who thought themselves secure, distressed under siege by famine and pestilence and the enemy, and more when the place was stormed and a breach made.

Calvin insists on the true commander. Though the Assyrians or Chaldeans attacked, God would be the principal leader of the war, and he claims here for himself what the Jews transferred to their earthly enemies. The blindness is a judgment fitted to the offence: they were so inflated with pride that they heedlessly despised all the prophets, and being wise in themselves they are given blindness, so that void of counsel they stumble and cannot proceed, seeing no end to their evils and finding no means of escape, held as it were fast bound. Wesley says it briefly, not knowing where to go, and Clarke as perplexing doubt and uncertainty, in which state their blood is poured out by the sword and their flesh trodden under foot. Ellicott glosses the groping as fancied insecurity and traces the metaphor to the curses of the law; the blood is poured out as recklessly as dust and the flesh cast aside like the vilest refuse, a sentence he compares with the burial of an ass pronounced on Jehoiakim. Wesley catches the double force of the comparison, as abundantly and as carelessly as dust in the highway. Calvin reads the reason clause as the whole point: the intermediate causes are not to be considered, for there is a higher one, contempt of God and of his celestial truth, and the words remind the Jews that no alleviation was to be expected when they had not only men hostile to them but God himself.

Gill ties the last verse back to the men on their lees, since the silver and gold gotten unjustly and hoarded were the very lees they were settled on; now they are disregarded by the Lord, unable to atone for sin or appease wrath, and of no avail with enemies who could not be bribed to spare their lives, as was said also of the Medes at the taking of Babylon. Clarke adds that they had expected happiness from that wealth. Calvin allows the ordinary force of the objection, that the most savage enemies are sometimes pacified by money, since avarice mitigates cruelty; but where God rules the war there is no redemption, and no way into favour except by repentance. Men dare not resist him openly, he says, and so hope by winding courses to avert his judgment, heaping their gold and silver into mountains, and none of it turns aside his hand. The fire is chosen for the same reason: no agreement can be made while fire rages, and the more materials there are the more the fire increases. On the last clause the voices part. Calvin judges that quickness rather than terror is meant, and objects to the received rendering of the noun, preferring a full end or consummation. Ellicott renders it that he shall effect a destruction, yea a terrible one, and thinks the phrasing borrowed from an earlier prophet. Wesley closes with the moral: let not sinners be laid asleep by the patience of God, for when the measure of their iniquity is full his justice will both overtake and overcome them, and make quick and thorough work.
